title: Computer and learning foundations
summary: How a computer runs your code, how to move around a terminal, and how to keep your work safe with Git.

units.title: Files, paths and the terminal
outcomes: You can navigate folders with cd, ls and pwd and explain absolute versus relative paths.
You can run a program from the terminal and redirect its output to a file.

learn.title: MIT Missing Semester — Lecture 1: Course overview + the shell
learn.slice: Lecture 1 (full, ~48 min) plus the lecture notes

read.title: The Linux Command Line (free book) — Chapter 2: Navigation

practice.title: Build a tidy learning folder
practice.brief: Create ~/learning with notes/ and code/ subfolders using only the terminal. Write hello.py into code/, run it, and save the output to notes/run.txt with redirection.
practice.done_when: notes/run.txt contains your program's output and you can paste the exact commands you used.

quiz.prompt: You are in /home/sam/learning. Which path points to /home/sam/learning/code/hello.py?
quiz.explain: A relative path starts from the working directory, so code/hello.py resolves inside /home/sam/learning.

options: Prints to the screen and to out.txt
Writes standard output to out.txt, replacing its contents
quiz.explain: > redirects standard output and truncates the file; >> would append.

quiz.prompt: Which command tells you the current working directory?
Explain the difference between your editor and your terminal, and when you use each.
rubric: The editor is where you write and save source files
The terminal is where you run commands and programs
Saving a file does not run it; running happens in the terminal

units.title: Version control with Git
outcomes: You can create a repository, commit changes with clear messages and push to GitHub.
You can explain what a commit and a branch are.

learn.title: MIT Missing Semester — Lecture 6: Version Control (Git)

practice.title: Put your learning folder on GitHub
practice.brief: Turn ~/learning into a Git repository, make three commits with meaningful messages and push it to a public GitHub repo.
practice.done_when: The repo is public and shows at least three commits.

quiz.prompt: What does a Git commit store?
options: A snapshot of the tracked files plus metadata
A copy of your whole disk
quiz.explain: Git stores snapshots (trees of blobs) with author, time, message and parent pointers.

quiz.prompt: Which command uploads your local commits to GitHub?
quiz.explain: git push sends local commits to the remote.

options: A full copy of the repository
A movable pointer to a commit
quiz.explain: Branches are lightweight references to commits.

quiz.prompt: Why are small commits with clear messages useful?
rubric: Easy to understand what changed and why
Easy to undo or bisect one change
Helps reviewers and your future self

capstone.title: Your learning workspace
capstone.brief: Publish a GitHub repo that holds your notes and first programs, with a README that explains how to run them from a terminal.
